name.text: L9 Q1 GitOps and continuous delivery

generalfeedback.text: GitOps is continuous delivery applied to a different type of code: infrastructure, configuration, and operations code kept in Git and delivered through automation. It is not limited to Kubernetes; servers, cloud resources, and other infrastructure can be managed the same way. Git hosting services provide the pipelines, but GitOps is the practice rather than the service, and it is not a branching model.

answer.text: As a Kubernetes-only practice in which an agent in the cluster applies manifests from Git
As continuous delivery applied to infrastructure and operations code kept in Git
As a hosted service that stores repositories and runs their pipelines in one place
As a branching model in which each environment gets its own long-lived Git branch

questiontext.text: In a pull-based GitOps setup, how do changes reach the infrastructure?

generalfeedback.text: In the pull model, a component running inside or near the infrastructure, such as a Puppet agent, ansible-pull, or Argo CD, periodically pulls the repository and applies the changes. Because it lives close to the infrastructure, it holds the permissions there. A pipeline that connects to the targets is the push model, and changes applied by hand or from a laptop bypass automated delivery.

answer.text: A pipeline in the hosted Git service connects to each target and pushes the change
An engineer pulls the repository to a laptop and applies the change from there
An agent in or near the infrastructure regularly fetches the repository and applies it
Each target server waits until an operator copies the new files onto it by hand

questiontext.text: The platform team owns its infrastructure repository. An application team opens a pull request there with a change it needs. Who merges that change into the main branch?

generalfeedback.text: The team that owns a repository defines its structure, pipelines, and rules, and only it can push or merge to the main branch. Other teams submit pull requests; the pipeline checks them without deploying, and the owners review the green request and merge it, which triggers delivery. The pipeline informs the decision but does not replace the owners, and the aim is to avoid slow, central approval paths.

answer.text: The team that wrote the change, as soon as its pull request passes the pipeline checks
The pipeline itself, which merges each pull request automatically once its checks are green
A central change board, which approves merges for every repository in the organization
The platform team that owns the repository, after it reviews the checked pull request

questiontext.text: A team keeps declarative infrastructure code in Git and delivers every merged change through a pipeline. It has no controller that continuously reconciles the infrastructure with Git; instead, it runs the pipeline on a schedule to detect and fix drift. Many GitOps definitions list continuous reconciliation as a fourth principle. How does this setup relate to GitOps?

generalfeedback.text: The setup has the three core principles: declarative code, versioned and immutable code in Git, and automatic delivery. A fourth principle, a desired state controller that keeps checking the target against Git, is optional: GitOps works without it, and scheduled pipeline runs give much of the same verification, though only at each run rather than continuously. GitOps is not limited to Kubernetes, scheduled runs correct drift rather than cause it, and the desired state stays in Git.

answer.text: It is not GitOps, because GitOps needs a controller running inside a Kubernetes cluster
It covers the core of GitOps, and the scheduled runs give part of what continuous reconciliation would
It is not GitOps, because a pipeline that applies changes on a schedule causes drift
It is GitOps only if the infrastructure stores the desired state itself instead of Git

questiontext.text: A team runs its pipelines on a public hosted CI/CD service. The pipelines run provisioning and configuration tools that connect to the company's private infrastructure and push each change there. What must the team take care of in this push model?

generalfeedback.text: In the push model, the CI/CD service runs tools such as Terraform, Ansible, or Helm and connects directly to the infrastructure, so it needs network access and credentials for the targets. When the CI/CD service is public rather than internal, that access must be secured carefully. Pull requests and commit history work the same way in both models, and either model can work, depending on the tools and security requirements.

answer.text: Giving the CI/CD service network access and credentials for the targets, and keeping that access secure
Nothing extra, because a pull model needs exactly the same access to the infrastructure
Replacing pull requests with direct commits to the main branch, because pushed changes bypass review
Keeping a separate change log, because a pushed change leaves no record in the repository

questiontext.text: Why can a repository's CI/CD pipeline be called guardrails for the team that owns the repository?

generalfeedback.text: The pipeline's checks, such as syntax, policy, security, and vulnerability checks, block any change that breaks the owning team's rules. The pipeline definition is code stored in the same repository and maintained by that team, so it codifies the team's knowledge. Pull request pipelines verify without deploying, and the owners still review complex or risky changes, but much of the routine review is delegated to automation.

answer.text: It deploys each pull request to production at once, so users find mistakes quickly.
It replaces human review, so owners no longer look at changes that other teams propose.
Its checks block changes that break the owners' rules, codifying what the owners know.
It is maintained by a central platform team, so the owners cannot weaken its checks.

name.text: L9 Q7 A complete record of change

questiontext.text: After an outage, a team must find out which change reached production, who approved it, and whether its checks passed. Some recent changes were applied from engineers' laptops. Which practice gives the team a complete record in future?

generalfeedback.text: The commit history shows who changed what and why, the pull request shows the review, and the pipeline logs show when each change ran and with what result; observability then shows the state of the infrastructure. The record is complete only when automation is the single path for changes. Changes applied from laptops or directly by senior engineers bypass it, and chat messages or snapshots do not show who approved a change or whether its checks passed. Emergency access, if a team needs it, should still leave a commit afterwards, so that the code and the record catch up with the change.

answer.text: Deliver every change through reviewed commits and the pipeline, whose logs record each run.
Ask engineers to post a summary in the team chat whenever they apply a change from a laptop.
Take a snapshot of production every night, and compare snapshots when an incident happens.
Keep the pipeline for routine work, but let senior engineers apply urgent changes directly.

name.text: L9 Q8 Replacing tickets with pull requests

questiontext.text: A database team often needs small network changes, such as an opened port or a new route, in the network team's infrastructure repository. Today each request goes through tickets and takes days of back-and-forth for a change of a few lines. The company moves to GitOps so that the database team can make such changes itself, as self-service, while the network team keeps control of its network. Which workflow fits best?

generalfeedback.text: In GitOps, self-service means pull requests to the owning team's repository instead of the back-and-forth of tickets between teams. The owners' pipeline checks each request automatically and gives feedback without deploying; the owners review a green request when they can and merge it, and the merge delivers the change. The owners keep control of the main branch while delegating implementation to the requesting team and much of the review to automation. Direct device access or direct pushes remove that control, and batching tickets keeps the delays.

answer.text: Give the database team administrator access to the network devices, so it can make small changes itself and inform the network team afterwards.
Let the database team push to the main branch of the network repository, so its changes deploy at once and the network team reviews them later.
Let the database team open pull requests whose pipeline checks run without deploying; the network team reviews green ones and merging deploys them.
Keep the tickets, but have the network team collect them for a weekly maintenance window, so that the requested changes are reviewed together.

name.text: L9 Q9 Layer repositories and simple interfaces

questiontext.text: An organization keeps its infrastructure in one repository per layer (network, machine images, server configuration, and application deployment), each owned by one team. Other teams often need to add simple entries, such as DNS records or batch jobs, to layers they do not own, while the owners keep refactoring the internals. Which organization best supports both kinds of change?

generalfeedback.text: The owning team stays responsible for the complex internals of its layer, but changes that other teams need often should be easy to make: simple interface files such as YAML or JSON in the repository, sometimes a separate repository or a self-service portal, changed through pull requests that the owners' pipeline checks. In one real case, batch jobs moved into a repository that the data warehouse team could change under policy and security checks, which ended the waiting. A shared repository without owners, private copies, and tickets for every change each lose either control or flow.

answer.text: Merge the layers into one repository that every team can change directly, so no team waits for an owner to act.
Keep the internals with the owners, and expose simple data files that others change through checked pull requests.
Let each team copy the layers it needs into its own repository and apply its copy independently of the owners.
Freeze the internals and route outside requests through tickets, so that the owners make every change themselves.
